Security Dispatch

A 20-Minute Kernel Patch for Ubuntu Relays

Dropping IPv4 packets with IP options keeps hosts alive against remote execution.

Relay operators moved quickly this weekend to mitigate CVE-2026-98432, a Linux kernel vulnerability tied to Multipath TCP that allows remote code execution [s561].

With upstream Ubuntu kernels still unpatched, hasky published a verified mitigation strategy [s564]: one nftables rule dropping IPv4 TCP packets with IP options alongside disabling MPTCP, anchored in a reboot-proof systemd unit. As hasky urged operators on Friday: If you run a relay or a node on Ubuntu, this is a 20-minute job. Do it today.

FOSS & Cyberspace

Two Truths and the FOSS Subsidy Deficit

By Gigi

Highlighting reflections on software freedom, Gigi marked passages detailing the fragile economic reality of open source [s534]: My hope is that OpenSats will eventually become obsolete. Until it is, we are dependent on donors who believe, like we do, that free and open-source software is paramount to a free and prosperous society.

The stark math remains: the reality is that less than 1% of users who benefit from the FOSS ecosystem give back to it, financially or otherwise [s537]. Yet the cypherpunk foundation holds firm on two fundamental truths: 1) code is speech, speech is information, and information is notoriously hard to stifle. 2) Strong cryptography empowers individuals and disempowers oppressors, inverting hierarchies that have stood for millennia. [s544]

Lead Story

The Billion-Dollar Signing Machine

A single laptop breach at Binance cost $6.3 billion across ten chains, while self-custody and node hardening take center stage on the eighteenth anniversary of the Bitcoin whitepaper.

At 20:05 UTC on October 29, hot wallets belonging to Binance began draining in the largest cryptocurrency heist on record [s556]. Within twenty minutes, approximately $6.3 billion vanished across ten blockchains, including 18,270 bitcoin. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs attributed the operation with high confidence to the North Korean state hacking group TraderTraitor [s556].

Crucially, private keys were never leaked or extracted. Instead, an attacker infiltrated a DevOps engineer's laptop, jumped into an internal service container, and commandeered Binance's own automated hot-wallet signing system to sign unauthorized withdrawal batches [s556, s559]. Co-CEO Richard Teng confirmed that investigators later uncovered additional points of compromise [s559, s561].

The aftermath drew an immediate contrast between centralized stablecoins and base-layer sound money. Centralized issuers froze an estimated $2.67 billion to $3 billion in dollar tokens within hours—Tether locking down 971 million USDT in just 37 minutes [s559]. But nobody froze the 18,270 bitcoin [s556, s559]. As observers noted, the same unilateral power that halts a state-sponsored hacker can halt any citizen without recourse [s556].

The theft arrives thirteen months after the cycle's peak, echoing past bear-market collapses like Mt. Gox, QuadrigaCX, and FTX [s556]. Yet with Binance pledging corporate reserves to cover all client balances and aiming to resume withdrawals on Sunday [s561], network sentiment turned from panic to practical self-custody.

Pilgrimage & Tradition

Henro Completed on Shikoku

Thirty-seven days walking eighty-eight temples across the Japanese island.

On the southern island of Shikoku, TJ.III concluded the traditional 88-temple Henro pilgrimage after more than a month on foot [s44]. As TJ.III posted upon completing the loop: FOR 37 DAYS IVE WORN VARIOUS PARTS OF THE HENRO COSTUME. WITH HONOR. TODAY THE COSTUME IS PACKED AWAY AND I HIKE AS ME. THE LAST DAY ON THE PILGRIMAGE. JUST A DUDE WALKING [s44].
